Unit 0 · Start here How this tutor works Every exercise on this site runs against a real git repository in your browser. Nothing is simulated, and nothing you type can hurt anything. Before you start You've used git — you commit, branch, push, and you've googled your way out of at least one mess. That's the level this course starts from. It spends its time on the half of git that most people never get taught: rewriting history on purpose, the object database underneath, digging through the past, and the collaboration commands that stop you losing other people's work. The idea The awkward thing about learning advanced git is that the interesting commands are the frightening ones. Nobody wants to practise rebase --onto on the repository they get paid to look after, so most people learn these commands the hard way — at 6pm, on a branch that matters, from a Stack Overflow answer written in 2013. So this site gives you a repository to break instead. Each page comes with a sandbox: a small history, already committed, with a prompt attached. You type real git commands, they really run, and the graph beside them really moves. When you wreck it, a button puts it back. It really is git That claim is worth being precise about, because a fake would teach you wrong. The engine here is isomorphic-git , a full reimplementation of git in JavaScript, writing to a filesystem that lives in your browser's storage. It writes real objects , hashed with SHA-1 exactly as git hashes them, into real .git/objects/ directories, with real refs in .git/refs/ . The proof is in the repository this site is built from: scripts/verify-fixtures.js builds every sandbox history with this engine, then hands the result to the actual git binary. Real git runs fsck --strict over it, agrees on every ref, and — given the same author and timestamps — produces the same commit, tree and blob ids . The object ids you're about to see are the ids git would have made. Where the tutor adds its own code, and why that

h: The details (open as much as you like)
b: Unit 0 · Start here The one mental model Four sentences of theory that make every command in the four units after this one predictable instead of memorised. Before you start Nothing beyond having used git. If you can already say what a branch is made of, skim to Try it and move on. The idea Here it is, all of it: The whole model A commit is a complete snapshot of your project, plus a pointer to the commit that came before it. A branch is a sticky note with one commit's name on it. HEAD is a sticky note saying which branch you're standing on. Almost every git command is a way of moving one of those notes. Two consequences do most of the work in this course. Commits are snapshots, not diffs. Git shows you diffs because diffs are what humans want to read, but it stores whole trees. When you hear that a rebase "replays your changes", what actually happens is that git computes a diff between two snapshots, applies it somewhere else, and stores the resulting snapshot. The diff is a means, not the data. History points backwards. A commit names its parent; a parent knows nothing about its children. So "the commits on this branch" is never a list git looks up — it's the answer to a walk, starting at the sticky note and following parents until it runs out. Everything follows from that: Deleting a branch deletes a sticky note. The commits are untouched — they have simply become unreachable , which is why they can be recovered. You cannot edit a commit. Its name is a hash of its contents, parent included, so changing anything makes a different commit. Every "rewrite" command builds new commits and moves a sticky note to them. Changing one commit changes every commit after it, because each one's hash includes its parent's hash. Rewriting the tip is cheap; rewriting the root rewrites everything. Try it The sandbox below has two branches. Watch what git branch -D does and doesn't destroy — the goals check that the commits outlived the branch that named them. Useful here: git log -

h: The details (open as much as you like)
b: Unit 1 · Internals & plumbing Blobs, trees and commits One walk, from a commit id down to a file's bytes, with cat-file the whole way. After this the object graph is something you can navigate rather than something you've read about. The idea Three object types stack into everything git knows: blob bytes. No name, no permissions, no history. tree a list of entries: mode name id . The id is a blob (a file) or another tree (a subdirectory). commit one tree id, zero or more parent ids, an author, a committer, a message. So a commit doesn't contain your files; it names one tree, which names blobs and further trees. "The state of the project at commit X" is a walk, and it is a walk you can do by hand: git cat-file -p HEAD # the commit: find its "tree" line git cat-file -p <tree id> # the root directory listing git cat-file -p <blob id> # a file's contents Try it Do that walk in the sandbox. The fixture has a file inside a subdirectory, so you'll pass through two trees on the way down. The object explorer below the prompt does the same thing with clicks if you'd rather see it laid out. Then try the shortcut git gives you for the same journey: git ls-tree -r HEAD # every blob in the commit, recursively git rev-parse HEAD^{tree} # the tree id, without reading the commit git cat-file -p HEAD:notes/plan.md # straight to one file's contents The details (open as much as you like) Reading a tree entry A tree prints like this: 100644 blob 8d0e41234f24b6da002d962a26c2495ea16a425f hello.txt 040000 tree 4d5fcadc293a348e88f777dc0920f11e7d71441c notes The number is the mode , and git stores only a handful: Note what's missing: no owner, no group, no read/write bits, no timestamps. Git records the executable bit and nothing else, which is why "the permissions changed after clone" is never a git bug. Inside a commit object git cat-file -p HEAD prints the object nearly verbatim: tree b63a1aea7985e1741ecf1d833a25ed164eef0503 parent 26a52436a5b6d5a24e2b1c8cebc0eb0d4b6e2f9a author Ada River

h: The details (open as much as you like)
b: Unit 1 · Internals & plumbing A commit, by hand Build a commit with four plumbing commands and no git commit anywhere. This is the page that makes the rest of git stop being magic. Before you start This page uses everything in Unit 1: objects, trees, the index and refs. It's the payoff for them, so it's worth having read them first. The idea git commit is a wrapper. Underneath, it does four things, each of which is a separate command you can run yourself: 1 git hash-object -w <file> store the contents as a blob 2 git update-index --add … put that blob at a path in the index 3 git write-tree turn the index into a tree object 4 git commit-tree <tree> -p <parent> -m … make a commit object pointing at that tree 5 git update-ref refs/heads/… move the branch to it Notice where the boundary falls. Steps 1–4 only add objects; nothing about your repository's visible state changes. Only step 5 moves a ref — and that is the step that makes the commit part of history. A commit object that no ref reaches is exactly what "dangling" means, and you can create one on purpose here. This split is not trivia. It's why the reflog can undo things, why rebase is implementable at all, and why commit-tree is what tools like filter-repo are built out of. Try it Work through it in the sandbox, pasting each id into the next command: echo "print('hi')" > hi.py git hash-object -w hi.py # → blob id git update-index --add hi.py # index now proposes it git write-tree # → tree id git commit-tree <tree id> -p HEAD -m "Add hi.py" # → commit id git log --oneline # nothing changed! the commit is unreferenced git update-ref refs/heads/main <commit id> git log --oneline # now it's history Between the fourth and sixth commands you have a real commit that no branch can see. git cat-file -p it, and try git fsck --no-reflogs before you run update-ref . h: The details (open as much as you like)
b: Unit 1 · Internals & plumbing Objects and hashes Git is a key-value store where the key is the hash of the value. Once you have typed that hash out by hand, half of git's behaviour stops being surprising. The idea Git stores four kinds of object : a blob (a file's contents), a tree (a directory listing), a commit, and an annotated tag . Each one is stored under a key, and the key is the SHA-1 hash of the object itself. That's the whole storage layer. The hash isn't taken over the file's bytes alone. Git prefixes a header — the type, a space, the length in bytes, and a zero byte — and hashes the lot: sha1("blob " + <length> + "\0" + <contents>) So a 12-byte file containing hello world\n is hashed as the 17 bytes blob 12\0hello world\n . You can reproduce this outside git with any SHA-1 tool, and people do, as a sanity check. Being content-addressed has consequences you rely on daily: Identical content is stored once, however many commits or branches contain it. An id cannot lie about what it names. Corruption is detectable: rehash the object and compare. Nothing can be edited in place. Every command that appears to modify history actually writes new objects — which is why so much of what looks destroyed is merely unnamed. Try it Type this in the sandbox and watch the id show up as a filename: echo "hello world" > hello.txt git hash-object hello.txt # compute the id, store nothing git hash-object -w hello.txt # compute it and write the object ls .git/objects/ # the first two hex characters are the directory git cat-file -t <paste the id> # what type is it? git cat-file -p <paste the id> # print it back Note what did not happen: nothing was committed, nothing was staged, and git status still shows an untracked file. You put an object in the database directly. The details (open as much as you like) Where the object actually lands An id like 3b18e512dba79e4c8300dd08aeb37f8e728b8dad becomes the path .git/objects/3b/18e512dba79e4c8300dd08aeb37f8e728b8dad The two-character

h: The details (open as much as you like)
b: Unit 1 · Internals & plumbing Refs, HEAD and symbolic refs Branches are one-line text files. Once you have edited one with echo, the difference between checkout, reset and branch -f stops mattering very much. The idea An object id is 40 characters of hex, so git gives you names for the ones you care about. A ref is a name holding one object id, stored as a file: .git/refs/heads/main → a branch .git/refs/tags/v1.0 → a tag .git/refs/remotes/origin/main → a remote-tracking ref Each contains one line: a 40-character id and a newline. That's it. A branch is not a container, a list, or a lineage — it is a filename with a hash in it. HEAD is the interesting one, because it usually doesn't contain an id at all: $ cat .git/HEAD ref: refs/heads/main That's a symbolic ref — a ref pointing at another ref. It's the indirection that makes committing work: git commit updates whatever ref HEAD names, so the branch moves and HEAD follows for free. Try it Read the files yourself, then move a branch by writing to one. The .git tab under the prompt shows every ref and the contents of HEAD as you go. cat .git/HEAD cat .git/refs/heads/main git symbolic-ref HEAD # the polite way to read it git update-ref refs/heads/spike HEAD~2 # make a branch with plumbing git checkout --detach HEAD~1 # now look at .git/HEAD again cat .git/HEAD The details (open as much as you like) Why checkout is two different operations git checkout main writes ref: refs/heads/main into HEAD and updates your files. git checkout <commit> writes the raw id instead. That single difference is detached HEAD , and it explains the behaviour that follows from it: committing works, but nothing is following you, so the commits become unreachable as soon as you leave. Modern git splits the two jobs into two commands — git switch for branches, git restore for files — precisely because checkout doing both is how people accidentally throw away uncommitted work. packed-refs, and refs that aren't files A repository with thousands of

h: The details (open as much as you like)
b: Unit 1 · Internals & plumbing Revision syntax ~ and ^, two dots and three, @{1} and @{u}. The notation experienced git users trade without ever having been taught it out loud. The idea Every command that takes a commit takes this grammar, so learning it once pays off everywhere. Two rules cover most of it. ~ goes back. ^ picks a parent. For an ordinary commit with one parent they're the same thing, which is why people use them interchangeably and then get surprised at a merge: HEAD~ the first parent — one step back HEAD~3 three steps back, always taking the first parent HEAD^ the first parent. Same as HEAD~ HEAD^2 the second parent. Only a merge commit has one HEAD~2^2 two back, then the second parent of that So on a merge commit, HEAD^ is the branch you were on and HEAD^2 is the branch you merged in. HEAD~2 is not "two commits ago" in any general sense — it's two steps down the first-parent line, ignoring everything that was merged in. Two dots is a range; three dots is "how we diverged". main..feature commits in feature that aren't in main — "my branch's own work" main...feature commits in either but not both — the full picture of the divergence ^main feature the long form of main..feature , and it takes any number of terms The one that trips people up: git diff a..b and git diff a b mean the same thing, but git log a..b and git log a b do not. For log , a range is a set of commits to walk; for diff , it's just two endpoints. Try it The sandbox has diverged branches, so all of this has something to bite on: git log --oneline --all git rev-parse HEAD~2 git rev-parse main..feature # try it: what does rev-parse make of a range? git rev-list --count main..feature git rev-list --left-right --oneline main...feature git show :/README # find a commit by its message git rev-parse HEAD^{tree} The details (open as much as you like) @{…} — asking about the past instead of the graph Everything above navigates the commit graph. The @{…} family navigates the reflog instead, whic

h: The details (open as much as you like)
b: Unit 1 · Internals & plumbing The index, properly The index isn't a queue of changes — it's a complete proposed snapshot. That one correction fixes most confusion about staging. The idea People picture the index as a list of changes waiting to be committed. It is actually a full flat list of every path in your project, each with a blob id and some cached file stats: $ git ls-files -s 100644 8d0e41234f24b6da002d962a26c2495ea16a425f 0 README.md 100644 151e2f818f2f6a619a0049dec48becf86b836ca7 0 count.py Read that as a proposed tree. git commit doesn't gather your changes; it turns the index into a tree object and points a commit at it. That's why git write-tree works at any moment, and why an empty git add session still produces a complete snapshot. So git status is two comparisons against this middle thing: index vs HEAD "Changes to be committed" working tree vs index "Changes not staged for commit" in neither "Untracked files" And it explains the situation everyone hits: a file can appear in both lists at once. You staged version 2, then edited it into version 3. The index holds v2, disk holds v3, and committing gets you v2 — which is a feature, and the entire basis of git add -p . Try it The sandbox starts dirty on purpose: one staged change, one unstaged, one untracked file. Take it apart: git status git ls-files -s # the index as a proposed snapshot git diff # worktree vs index git diff --staged # index vs HEAD git write-tree # the tree the index would become git cat-file -p <that tree id> # a real tree object that isn't in any commit Then stage the README edit, edit it again before committing, and look at git status . Both lists mention it. The details (open as much as you like) The stat cache, and why status is fast Each index entry stores the file's size and modification time as of the last add . To answer "did this file change?", git compares stats first and only reads the file if they differ. That's how git status stays quick in a repository with 100,000 file

h: The details (open as much as you like)
b: Unit 2 · History rewriting Amending the last commit git commit --amend doesn't edit your commit. It builds a replacement and abandons the original — and everything else in this unit is that same move, at larger scale. The idea You commit, then notice the typo. git commit --amend fixes it, and the mental model most people carry away is "amend edits the last commit". It can't. A commit's id is a hash of its contents, so an edited commit is a different commit. What actually happens: Git builds a new commit from the current index, with the same parent as the old one and whatever message you give. It moves your branch to the new commit. The old commit is now unreachable . It is still there, byte for byte, named in the reflog . Two useful consequences fall straight out. An amend is always recoverable — git reset --hard HEAD@{1} puts you back. And an amend is a rewrite : if you already pushed, your branch and the remote's now disagree about a commit that exists in both, which is why the next push is rejected. Try it git log --oneline git commit --amend -m "A better message" git log --oneline # same position, different id git reflog # both ids are here: the new one and the old git cat-file -p HEAD@{1} # the "gone" commit, still perfectly readable Amending content works the same way: stage something first, and it joins the replacement commit instead of becoming a new one. The details (open as much as you like) Amend keeps the author, replaces the committer The new commit inherits the original's author name, email and date, and gets you and now as committer . So git log still shows the original date while git log --format=%cd shows today. This is the same mechanism as cherry-pick and rebase — anything that replays a commit preserves authorship and records who moved it. Use --reset-author when you genuinely wrote it now, which mostly matters when you're amending someone else's commit. h: The details (open as much as you like)
b: Unit 2 · History rewriting Cherry-pick Copying one commit somewhere else. The mechanism is a three-way merge, which explains both why it usually just works and why the duplicate it leaves behind can bite you later. The idea You have a fix on one branch and you need it on another. git cherry-pick <commit> applies what that commit changed, here, and commits the result. "What that commit changed" is computed, not stored. Git does a three-way merge with: base the commit's parent — the world before it theirs the commit itself — the world after it ours where you are now That's why a cherry-pick can succeed even when the surrounding code has changed a lot: the merge only needs to reconcile the one region the commit touched. And it's why a conflict here looks exactly like a merge conflict — it is one. The result is a new commit with a new id : same author, same message, same tree change, different parent. The original stays where it was. You now have the same change twice in your project's history, under two names. Try it The sandbox has a hotfix branch with one commit you want on main : git log --oneline --all git checkout main git cherry-pick hotfix git log --oneline # a new id, the same subject git show HEAD # same change git cherry-pick -x hotfix~0 # try -x and read the message it writes The details (open as much as you like) -x, and why backports need it git cherry-pick -x appends a line to the message: (cherry picked from commit 961c4c8…) It costs nothing and it's the only durable record of where the change came from — the new commit has no structural link to the original. On a maintenance branch six months later, that line is the difference between "this was backported from main" and a mystery. Git doesn't do it by default because on a shared feature branch the referenced id may be one you rewrote away, making the note misleading. Rule of thumb: use it when picking from a permanent branch, skip it when picking from something you'll rebase. Duplicates, and what git ca
Get the hotfix commit onto main so the message records where it came from — and leave the hotfix branch exactly where it is.

h: The details (open as much as you like)
b: Unit 2 · History rewriting Interactive rebase The todo list is a file, the commands are a tiny language, and the whole thing is cherry-pick in a loop. Once you've seen the file, rebase -i stops being the scary one. Before you start Cherry-pick , because that is literally what each step of a rebase does. The idea git rebase -i <upstream> does three things in order: Works out which commits are yours — the range <upstream>..HEAD — and writes them, oldest first, into a file: .git/rebase-merge/git-rebase-todo . Opens that file in your editor. You change it. That's the whole "interactive" part. Detaches HEAD onto the new base and works down the list, replaying each commit as instructed, then moves your branch to the result. The file looks like this: pick 88f724f wip report pick b23dc77 more wip pick 587bc61 fix typo, tidy up, works now # Commands: # p, pick = use commit as it is # r, reword = use commit, but edit the message # e, edit = stop here to amend the commit # s, squash = meld into the previous commit, keeping both messages # f, fixup = meld into the previous commit, discarding this message # d, drop = remove commit # x, exec = run a shell command # # Lines are executed from top to bottom. Three things about that file are worth internalising. It's ordered oldest first — the opposite of git log , which catches everyone once. Reordering the lines reorders history. And deleting a line drops the commit , which is why an accidentally empty file makes git say "Nothing to do" and abort rather than destroy your branch. Try it The sandbox is on feature/report , three messy commits ahead of main. Run git rebase -i HEAD~3 : an editor opens on the real todo file. Change the second and third pick to squash , save, and watch the graph. One difference here Real git opens a second editor after a squash , so you can write the combined message. This sandbox simply joins the messages together, which means the squashed commit ends up with the first commit's subject. Follow it with gi

h: The details (open as much as you like)
b: Unit 2 · History rewriting rebase --onto Rebase normally conflates two questions. --onto separates them: which commits to move, and where to put them. The idea git rebase main means two things at once: take the commits that aren't in main , and put them on top of main . Usually that's what you want, so the conflation goes unnoticed. It stops being what you want when your branch was started from the wrong place. Say you branched feature off feature-base , wrote three commits, and now feature-base is abandoned. A plain rebase onto main would replay everything not in main — including feature-base's commits, which you don't want. The three-argument form splits the question: git rebase --onto <newbase> <upstream> [<branch>] │ │ │ └── which commits: <upstream>..branch └── where they land So "move just my three commits onto main" is: git rebase --onto main feature-base feature Read it as: replay the commits after feature-base up to feature, on top of main. Once you can read that sentence off the command, --onto stops being intimidating. Try it The sandbox has main , feature (branched off an older main) and hotfix . Try both forms and compare: git log --oneline --all git checkout feature git rebase main # the ordinary form git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD # undo it git rebase --onto main HEAD~1 feature # move only the newest commit git log --oneline --all The second one is the other everyday use: dropping the older commits of your own branch by choosing an upstream inside it. The details (open as much as you like) The three uses worth remembering Transplant a branch git rebase --onto main old-base feature — my commits, onto main, ignoring the old base's Drop early commits git rebase --onto main~3 main~6 main — keep the last three, throw the middle away Excise one commit git rebase --onto <bad>~ <bad> — replay everything after the bad commit onto its parent, removing it from history That last one is the surgical alternative to revert : instead of adding a commit that undoes it, th

h: The details (open as much as you like)
b: Unit 2 · History rewriting Rebase versus merge Not a matter of taste, exactly. They record different claims about what happened, and only one of them is safe on history other people have. The idea Your branch and main have both moved. You need them combined. Two options, and they differ in what ends up in the repository: merge one new merge commit with two parents. Your commits keep their ids. History records that two lines of work existed and were joined. rebase your commits are rebuilt on top of main, with new ids. History records a single line, as though you had started from today's main. So merge preserves what happened, and rebase presents what you wish had happened. Both are legitimate. The interesting question is not which is nicer to read but which facts you're prepared to lose. Where the answer is not a matter of taste: Unpushed local work: rebase freely. Nobody has those commits, so replacing them costs nothing, and you get a history that's reviewable. Anything others have based work on: merge. Rebasing changes the ids they're building on, and their next pull will try to reconcile two copies of every commit. A long-lived shared branch: merge, and stop asking. The "clean history" argument is not worth the recovery work. Try it The sandbox has diverged branches. Do it both ways and compare the graphs — the shape is the argument: git checkout feature git merge main # a merge commit appears, two parents git log --oneline --graph git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD # undo git rebase main # same content, one line, new ids git log --oneline --graph Look at git log --oneline after each: the merge leaves your original ids in place, the rebase replaces every one of them. The details (open as much as you like) Fast-forward, and why --no-ff exists If your branch tip is already an ancestor of what you're merging, there is nothing to combine: git can just slide the ref forward. That's a fast-forward , and it produces no merge commit at all. --ff (default) fast-forward when possi

h: The details (open as much as you like)
b: Unit 2 · History rewriting Recovering with the reflog The reason none of this unit is dangerous. Every ref movement is written down, so almost every git accident is two commands from being undone. The idea Every time a ref moves, git appends a line to a log. HEAD's log is .git/logs/HEAD ; each branch has its own under .git/logs/refs/heads/ . A line looks like this: d1cf19b 587bc61 Ada Rivera <ada@example.com> 1709543400 +0000 commit: fix typo Old id, new id, who, when, why. That's the whole reflog — and because it records the id a ref moved away from , it is a list of every commit you have abandoned. So the recovery procedure for nearly everything is the same three steps: git reflog — read down the list until you recognise where you were. Note the id, or its HEAD@{n} address. git reset --hard <that> to go back, or git branch rescue <that> to give it a name without moving. The second option is the better instinct: putting a new branch on the lost commit can't make anything worse, and lets you look before you leap. Try it Destroy something, then get it back: git log --oneline git reset --hard HEAD~3 # three commits gone from the branch git log --oneline # confirmed gone git reflog # …and there they are git reset --hard HEAD@{1} # back git branch rescue HEAD@{2} # or name it instead of moving Then try the harder version: delete a branch entirely and recover it. The branch's own reflog goes with it, so you need HEAD's log — or git fsck . The details (open as much as you like) HEAD@{n} versus HEAD~n — the distinction that matters at 6pm HEAD~3 three commits back through parents . A question about the graph HEAD@{3} where HEAD pointed three movements ago. A question about your history of commands After a bad reset --hard , HEAD~1 walks further into the past you didn't want, and HEAD@{1} is your rescue. Two characters apart, opposite directions. The reflog also takes times: HEAD@{yesterday} , main@{2.hours.ago} . Useful when you know roughly when things were fine. What the

h: The details (open as much as you like)
b: Unit 2 · History rewriting reset versus revert Both undo. One rewrites history and one adds to it — and choosing wrong is how teams lose an afternoon. The idea Two questions, and the answers are unrelated: The distinction reset moves your branch to a different commit. History changes shape; the undone commits are no longer on the branch. revert makes a new commit that undoes an old one. History grows; nothing is removed. So the choice is not about safety — reset is perfectly safe on a branch nobody else has — it's about whether the commits are already somewhere else. If they are, reverting is the only honest option: rewriting would break everyone who already has them. The three resets reset takes a commit and moves up to three things to match it: --soft branch only index and worktree untouched, so the undone changes are all staged, ready to recommit --mixed branch + index the default. Changes survive in your files, unstaged --hard branch + index + worktree your files are overwritten. The one that discards work Two things it never does, both worth knowing precisely: it never touches untracked files (so reset --hard won't remove that build directory), and it never deletes commits from the object database (so the reflog can undo it). git reset --soft HEAD~3 is the useful one people don't know: three commits collapse into a fully staged change, and one git commit makes them one. That's a squash without a rebase. Try it git log --oneline git reset --soft HEAD~2 # look at git status: everything staged git reset --mixed HEAD # keep going: now unstaged git status git reset --hard HEAD # and now clean — the changes are gone from your files git reflog # every one of those moves is recorded git reset --hard HEAD@{3} # back to where you started The details (open as much as you like) Reverting a merge, and why it needs -m A merge commit has two parents, so "undo this commit" is ambiguous: undo relative to which side? git revert -m 1 <merge> keeps the first parent's line and undo

h: The details (open as much as you like)
b: Unit 2 · History rewriting Rewriting published history Sometimes you have to. Here's how to do it with the least damage, and how to recognise the times you shouldn't. The idea The rule everyone repeats is "never rewrite published history". As stated it's too strong — the real content is: The actual rule Rewriting a branch replaces its commits with new ones. Anyone who has the old commits keeps them, and their git will try to combine both copies. So the cost of a rewrite is paid by everyone who already pulled — which is fine if that's nobody, or if you tell them. Which gives you a decision procedure rather than a taboo: Your own unpushed work Rewrite freely. Nobody is affected. Your own pushed feature branch, no one else on it Rewrite and push --force-with-lease . Normal practice. A shared feature branch Rewrite only after saying so. Everyone else needs git reset --hard origin/<branch> afterwards. main, or any long-lived branch Don't. Use revert . The exception that overrides all of it: a secret got committed. Then the history must be rewritten, everywhere, and the credential must be rotated anyway — because anyone who cloned already has it, and no rewrite can reach their disk. Rotate first; rewrite second. Try it The sandbox has a remote whose main has moved on, and a local branch you've rewritten. Watch git refuse, and then do it properly: git log --oneline --all git fetch git status # ahead and behind: you've diverged git push # rejected, and read the hint carefully git push --force # works, and would trample whatever origin had Then reset the sandbox and try the same thing with --force-with-lease instead, which is the subject of its own page because the difference matters so much. The details (open as much as you like) The message to send when you do rewrite a shared branch Rewrites go wrong socially, not technically. What people need is the exact command to run: I've rebased feature/parser and force-pushed. If you have it checked out: git fetch origin git reset

h: The details (open as much as you like)
b: Unit 2 · History rewriting squash, fixup, autosquash The habit that makes review comments cheap: commit the fix now, marked for where it belongs, and let one rebase put everything in its place. The idea You're six commits into a branch and a reviewer points out a bug in the second one. The bad options are: amend the wrong commit, add a commit called "fix review comment" and leave the history messy, or stop everything and rebase interactively right now. The good option is a two-part habit. Now , commit the fix with a marker saying where it belongs: git commit --fixup=<the commit it fixes> which writes a commit whose subject is literally fixup! <that commit's subject> . You carry on working. Later , when you're ready to tidy up: git rebase -i --autosquash main Git reads the fixup! prefixes, moves each of those commits directly beneath the commit it names, and changes its command to fixup — before showing you the todo list. You confirm and it's done. Two variants: --fixup=X fold in, keep X's message. The everyday one --squash=X fold in, and combine both messages so you can edit them together Set git config --global rebase.autoSquash true and --autosquash becomes the default, at which point this is just how you work. Try it The sandbox already contains two marked commits — one fixup! and one squash! . Look at them, then let autosquash place them: git log --oneline git rebase -i --autosquash HEAD~5 # read the todo list carefully before saving: the lines have been reordered for you Compare it with git rebase -i HEAD~5 without --autosquash and see how much manual reordering you were spared. The details (open as much as you like) How git matches a fixup! to its target By subject text, not by id. fixup! Add the report attaches to the commit whose subject is Add the report . Consequences: Two commits with the same subject make the match ambiguous — git picks one, and it may not be yours. --fixup=<sha> is only a convenience for looking up that subject; what's stored is the tex

t: Lab: Let autosquash place two marked commits
b: Fold the fixup! and squash! commits into the commits they name, leaving three clean commits and no marker subjects — with all the content intact.

One of the four things git stores: a file's contents, a directory listing, a commit, or a tag. The unit of storage in git's database. Every object is stored under the SHA-1 hash of its own contents, which is why the same content is never stored twice and why an id can never disagree with what it names. The four types are blob, tree, commit and tag.

A file's contents, with no name and no history attached. The object type that stores file content. A blob knows nothing about its filename, its permissions or where it sits — a tree supplies all of that. Two identical files anywhere in history are one blob.

A directory listing: names, permissions, and the object each name points at. The object type that gives structure to blobs. Each entry has a mode, a name, and the id of a blob (a file) or another tree (a subdirectory). A commit points at exactly one tree: the complete state of the project at that moment.

A snapshot plus who made it, when, why, and what came before it. An object holding one tree id, zero or more parent commit ids, an author, a committer, and a message. Because the parent ids are part of the hashed content, changing any commit changes every commit after it — the fact that makes rewriting history a rebuild rather than an edit.

A tag that is its own object, with a tagger, a date and a message. Created by `git tag -a`. Unlike a lightweight tag — which is just a ref pointing at a commit — an annotated tag is a fourth kind of object that points at a commit and carries its own metadata, and can be signed.

A name that points at a commit — a branch, a tag, or a remote-tracking name. A file under .git/refs/ (or a line in .git/packed-refs) containing an object id. Branches are refs under refs/heads/, tags under refs/tags/, remote-tracking refs under refs/remotes/. Nearly every git command is, underneath, a way of moving a ref.

A movable name for one commit — and, by following parents, all of its history. A ref under refs/heads/. A branch holds exactly one commit id and moves forward when you commit on it. It is not a container of commits: deleting a branch deletes only the name, which is why the commits survive long enough for the reflog to find them.

Where you are: the commit you have checked out. A symbolic ref in .git/HEAD, normally containing `ref: refs/heads/<branch>` — so it points at a branch, which points at a commit. Committing moves the branch HEAD names, which is how HEAD comes along for the ride.

HEAD points straight at a commit instead of at a branch. The state after `git checkout <commit>`. Commits you make still get created, but no branch moves to include them, so they become unreachable the moment you leave — findable only through the reflog. Rebase and bisect both work in this state deliberately.

A ref that points at another ref instead of at a commit. HEAD is the one you meet daily: it contains a ref name, not an object id. `git symbolic-ref HEAD` reads it; writing it is how `git checkout <branch>` switches branches without touching a single file's content.

The list of exactly what your next commit will contain. A binary file, .git/index, holding a full flat list of paths with the blob id and file stats for each. `git add` writes into it; `git commit` turns it into a tree. It is the third of the three trees — HEAD, the index, the working tree — and most confusing git states are a disagreement between them.

The actual files on disk that you edit. The checked-out copy of your project. Git compares it against the index to tell you what is unstaged, and against HEAD to tell you what has changed since the last commit. `git reset --hard` is the one common command that overwrites it.

A local diary of every position a ref has held. Plain text under .git/logs/: one line per movement of a ref, with the old id, the new id, who moved it and why. It is what makes almost every git accident recoverable, because a commit dropped by reset, rebase or a deleted branch is still named in the log. It is local, private, and expires.

Where HEAD was just before the last big move. A file git writes before operations that move HEAD a long way — reset, rebase, merge, pull. `git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD` is the one-step undo for the operation you just regretted.

The commit that came before this one. Recorded inside the commit object. A normal commit has one parent, a merge commit has two or more, and the very first commit has none. The first parent is special: it is the branch you were on when you merged, and what `~` and --first-parent follow.

For a merge commit, the branch you were standing on when you merged. Parent number one. `HEAD~3` walks first parents only, and `git log --first-parent` shows the trunk's own story without every merged branch's commits mixed in.

A commit with more than one parent, joining two lines of history. What `git merge` creates when it can't fast-forward. Its tree is the combined result; its parents record both sides, which is what preserves the fact that the two branches existed.

The most recent commit both branches share. The common ancestor a three-way merge measures from: git compares each side against the base to work out what each side changed. `git merge-base a b` prints it.

Combining two versions by looking at what each changed from a common starting point. Compare base→ours and base→theirs. Where only one side changed a region, take that side; where both changed it the same way, take it once; where both changed it differently, that is a conflict. Merge, cherry-pick, revert and every step of rebase are all this operation.

Both sides changed the same lines differently, so git stops and asks you. Git writes both versions into the file between `<<<<<<<`, `=======` and `>>>>>>>` markers, leaves the path unstaged, and records the in-progress state in .git/. Resolving means editing the file, staging it, and continuing — the marker is a note to you, not a format git understands.

Moving a branch straight up to a commit that already contains it. When your branch tip is an ancestor of what you're merging, git can simply slide the ref forward without making a merge commit. `--no-ff` forces a merge commit anyway; `--ff-only` refuses anything else. The same test decides whether a push is allowed.

The update would drop commits the other side already has, so git refuses. The rejection you get pushing a rewritten branch: the remote's tip is not an ancestor of yours, so accepting your push would make its commits unreachable. Forcing overrides the check; --force-with-lease overrides it safely.

A commit you can reach by walking backwards from another one. Reachability is the relation nearly every git decision rests on: whether a merge can fast-forward, whether a push is safe, whether an object survives gc, what a range means. `git merge-base --is-ancestor a b` tests it.

Some ref can get to it by following parents and trees. An object is reachable if a walk from any ref arrives at it. Reachable objects are permanent; unreachable ones are candidates for garbage collection. Reflog entries also count as starting points, which is exactly why they buy you recovery time.

Still in the database, but no ref can find it any more. What a commit becomes after the branch naming it is deleted or moved off it. It still exists byte-for-byte until git prunes it, which is why recovery is usually possible — via the reflog if it's still listed there, via `git fsck --unreachable` if it isn't.

Unreachable, and nothing else unreachable points at it either. git fsck's word for the tip of an orphaned chain. The distinction from plain 'unreachable' is useful in practice: dangling commits are the heads of lost work, so they are the ones worth looking at first.

Checks the object database and lists what nothing points at. `git fsck` verifies that objects are well-formed and connected, and reports dangling and unreachable ones. With --no-reflogs it ignores the reflog as a starting point, which reveals what is genuinely stranded rather than merely unnamed.

One object stored as one compressed file. The simple storage form: .git/objects/ab/cdef… where the path is the object's own hash. Git periodically bundles many loose objects into a packfile to save space and speed up walks.

Many objects in one file, stored as differences from each other. The compact storage form, with an index file beside it for lookups. Objects in a pack are often kept as deltas against a similar object, which is why a repository with thousands of versions of one file stays small.

Tidies the object database, and eventually deletes what nothing points at. `git gc` packs loose objects and prunes unreachable ones older than a grace period (two weeks by default), after expiring old reflog entries. It is the only routine operation that actually destroys lost commits, which is why recovery is a race you almost always win.

The low-level commands git's own scripts are built from. hash-object, cat-file, write-tree, commit-tree, update-ref and friends: stable, scriptable, and unconcerned with being friendly. The commands you use daily — 'porcelain' — are convenience layers over these.

Replace the last commit with a new one. `git commit --amend` does not edit a commit — it cannot, because a commit's id is its content. It builds a new commit with the same parent and moves the branch to it, leaving the old one unreachable and recoverable from the reflog.

Building replacement commits and pointing the branch at them. What amend, rebase, cherry-pick and filter-repo all do. The originals are never modified; they are abandoned. This is why rewriting is safe on your own branch and rude on a shared one: everyone else's history still contains the commits you abandoned.

Replay your commits on top of a different starting point. For each commit in a range, git works out what it changed and applies that change onto a new base, creating a new commit with a new id. The result is a linear history that looks as if you had started from the newer base — a story that never actually happened, told more clearly.

A rebase where you get to edit the list of steps first. `git rebase -i` writes a todo list to .git/rebase-merge/git-rebase-todo and opens it in your editor. Changing a line's command — pick, reword, edit, squash, fixup, drop, exec — changes what happens to that commit. It is a small programming language for history.

The file that says what an interactive rebase will do, step by step. .git/rebase-merge/git-rebase-todo. Git reads it top to bottom, and rewrites it as it goes, so `--continue` after a conflict simply resumes where the file says it got to. Because it is a file, you can inspect it mid-rebase.

Fold a commit into the one before it, keeping both messages. A rebase todo command. The two commits become one whose tree is the later state and whose message you get to edit, combining both. Use fixup instead when the second message is just 'oops'.

Fold a commit into the one before it and throw its message away. Like squash without the message merge. `git commit --fixup=<commit>` writes a commit whose subject is `fixup! <that commit's subject>`, so a later `rebase --autosquash` knows where it belongs without you reordering anything.

Moves every fixup! commit under the commit it names, automatically. `git rebase -i --autosquash` reorders the todo list before showing it to you: each `fixup!`/`squash!` commit is placed directly after its target with its command changed. With rebase.autoSquash=true it is the default, and reviewing a branch becomes a two-command habit.

Says where the replayed commits should land, separately from which ones they are. `git rebase --onto <newbase> <upstream> [branch]` splits the two questions rebase normally conflates: `<upstream>..branch` chooses the commits, `<newbase>` chooses the destination. The tool for lifting a branch off the wrong parent.

Copy one commit's change onto the branch you're on. Applies the difference a commit made and commits the result — a new commit, with a new id, the same author and a new committer. `-x` records which commit it came from, which is the difference between a traceable backport and a mystery.

A new commit that undoes an old one, leaving the old one in place. The safe undo for history other people already have: it adds, rather than rewrites. `git revert <commit>` applies that commit's change backwards. Reverting a merge needs -m to say which side to keep.

Move the current branch, and optionally the index and your files with it. `--soft` moves the branch only; `--mixed` (the default) also makes the index match; `--hard` also overwrites the working tree. Untracked files are never touched by any of them. Nothing is deleted from the database, so the reflog can undo it.

Binary search through history for the commit that broke something. You mark one commit good and one bad; git checks out the middle one and asks. Each answer halves the range, so a thousand commits take about ten tests. `git bisect run <script>` does the answering for you when the test can be automated.

Shows which commit last touched each line of a file. Useful, and misleading by default: a rename or a move makes every line look new. `-M` follows lines moved within a file, `-C` follows lines copied from other files in the same commit, and `-L` limits the search to a range of lines.

Searches history for the commits where a string appeared or disappeared. `git log -S<string>` reports commits that changed how many times the string occurs — the ones that added or removed it. `-G<regex>` is broader: every commit whose diff mentions it at all. -S answers 'who introduced this', -G answers 'who touched this'.

Shelves your uncommitted changes so you can come back to them. Records the working tree and index as commits parented off HEAD, pointed at by the refs/stash ref, then cleans your worktree. Because they are ordinary commits, a lost stash is recoverable through the stash reflog. `-u` includes untracked files, which the default deliberately doesn't.

A second checkout of the same repository, in another directory. `git worktree add` gives you another working tree and another HEAD sharing one object database and one set of refs. Cheaper than a clone, and unlike stashing it lets you have two branches genuinely open at once. Two worktrees cannot have the same branch checked out.

A rule saying which ref maps to which, when you fetch or push. `<src>:<dst>`, optionally prefixed with + to allow a non-fast-forward update. `refs/heads/*:refs/remotes/origin/*` is the fetch refspec that fills in your remote-tracking refs; `git push origin :old` has an empty source, which is how a push deletes a remote branch.

Your local note of where a branch on the remote was, last time you looked. A ref under refs/remotes/, such as refs/remotes/origin/main. You never commit on it; fetch updates it. It is a cache, and its being a cache is the whole point: --force-with-lease compares against it to detect that someone else pushed.

The remote branch your branch is set up to compare itself against. Configured as branch.<name>.remote and branch.<name>.merge, and written `@{u}` or `@{upstream}`. It is what makes `git status` able to say 'ahead 2, behind 1' without you naming a branch.

Force-push, but only if the remote is still where you last saw it. Compares the remote's current tip against your remote-tracking ref and refuses if they differ. This is the difference between overwriting your own rewritten branch and silently deleting a colleague's commit — which is exactly what plain --force does.

Remembers how you resolved a conflict and replays it next time. 'Reuse recorded resolution'. With rerere.enabled, git records the conflict's pre-image and your resolution under .git/rr-cache/ and reapplies it automatically when it sees the same conflict again — which happens constantly when you rebase a long-lived branch repeatedly.

A pointer to one specific commit of another repository. A tree entry with mode 160000 — a 'gitlink' — naming a commit id, plus a .gitmodules file saying where to clone it from. The superproject records which commit, not which branch, which is the source of both its precision and its reputation.

Another project's files copied into a subdirectory of yours, history and all. The alternative to a submodule: the files are really in your tree, so a clone needs nothing extra, at the cost of a bigger repository and a more involved update procedure.

The number in a tree entry saying what kind of thing it is. 100644 a file, 100755 an executable file, 120000 a symlink, 040000 a subdirectory, 160000 a submodule. Git stores no other permissions — the executable bit is the only one that survives a clone.

A script git runs at a particular moment, which can refuse to continue. An executable in .git/hooks/ named for its moment: pre-commit, commit-msg, pre-push, post-checkout. A non-zero exit stops the operation. Hooks are not cloned, which is why teams distribute them separately.

Having only part of the repository's files in your working tree. The index knows about every path, but only the patterns you list get written to disk. Combined with a partial clone (which also skips downloading the blobs you don't need) it is how very large repositories stay workable.

Extra text attached to a commit without changing it. `git notes` stores annotations in refs/notes/commits, keyed by the commit they describe, so `git log` can display them. Because the commit itself is untouched, its id doesn't change — the only way to add to a commit after the fact.
say head. the commit you have checked out — normally via the branch you're on
say at. exactly the same thing as HEAD, two fewer keystrokes
say rev tilde. the first parent of <rev>. HEAD~ is the commit before HEAD
say rev tilde three. walk back 3 commits, always taking the first parent. HEAD~3 is three commits ago on this line of history
say rev caret. the same as <rev>~ for an ordinary commit: its first parent
say rev caret two. the second parent of a merge commit — the branch that was merged in. Only merge commits have one
say rev caret brace tree. the tree object of that commit, rather than the commit itself. HEAD^{tree} is the root directory of your last commit
say rev caret brace commit. follow tags until you reach an actual commit. Useful because an annotated tag is an object in its own right
say colon slash text. the newest commit whose message contains that text. :/fix typo finds it without you looking up an id
say the sha, or the hash. any unambiguous prefix of a full 40-character id — usually 7 characters is plenty

t: HEAD@{1} — at brace n — the nth reflog entry
b: say head at brace one. where HEAD pointed one move ago. HEAD@{0} is now, HEAD@{1} is before your last command — the undo button's address
say main at brace two. where the branch main pointed two of its own movements ago. Each ref has a separate log, so main@{2} and HEAD@{2} usually differ
say at brace minus one. the branch you were on before this one — what `git checkout -` uses
say at brace you, or at upstream. the remote-tracking branch your branch is set to compare against, usually origin/<same name>
say at brace push. the ref `git push` would update — the same as @{u} in ordinary setups, different under triangular workflows
say orig head. where HEAD was before the last big move (reset, rebase, merge, pull). `git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD` undoes it

t: A..B — two dots — in B but not A
b: say A dot dot B. the commits reachable from B that aren't reachable from A. main..feature is 'my branch's own commits'

t: A...B — three dots — in either but not both
b: say A dot dot dot B. the symmetric difference: everything either side has that the other doesn't. With --left-right, git marks which side each commit came from
say not A, B. the long form of a range: include B, exclude A. Takes any number of each, unlike ..
say rev caret bang. the commit and none of its ancestors — a range containing exactly one commit
say first parent. when walking, only ever follow parent number one — the trunk's own story, without the commits merged into it
say refs heads main. what the branch 'main' is really called. Branches live under refs/heads/
say refs tags v one point oh. tags live under refs/tags/ and, by convention, don't move
say refs remotes origin main. your local note of where origin's main was when you last fetched. Written origin/main for short
say refs stash. the ref pointing at your most recent stash. Its reflog holds the older ones — which is why a dropped stash is recoverable
say source colon destination. push or fetch the ref on the left into the ref on the right. `git push origin main:main` is the explicit form of the everyday push
say plus source colon destination. update even if it isn't a fast-forward. This is what --force does, written into the refspec itself
say colon destination. push nothing into that ref, which deletes it. `git push origin :old-branch` removes the remote branch
say wildcard refspec. every branch on the remote becomes a remote-tracking ref locally. This line in .git/config is why origin/* exists
say dash dash. everything after this is a path, not a revision. `git checkout -- file` means the file, even if a branch shares its name
say rev colon path. the blob for that path in that commit. `git show HEAD~2:src/app.py` prints the old version without checking anything out
say colon paren exclude. everything except this. `git log -- . ':(exclude)*.lock'` skips the noisy files
say one hundred six forty-four. a regular, non-executable file. The commonest thing in any tree
say one hundred seven fifty-five. a regular file with the executable bit set. The only permission git records
say one twenty thousand. the 'file' content is the path it points at
say forty thousand. the entry is another tree object
say one sixty thousand. a 'gitlink': the entry names a commit in another repository rather than any content in this one
